title: Energy stores and transfers
examTip: Energy questions appear on every exam paper. You need to name stores exactly and describe transfers correctly. You also need to use Sankey diagrams to work out efficiency. Learn the eight stores and four transfer pathways by heart.
introTips: There are exactly eight energy stores examiners expect you to name. The names matter. Say 'kinetic', not 'movement'. Say 'gravitational potential', not 'height energy'.
Energy is never created or destroyed. It only moves between stores or spreads out as heat. This is the law of conservation of energy. Every energy calculation you do is built on it.
Sankey diagrams are a common 2–3 mark question. The width of each arrow tells you the amount of energy. Here you will learn to read them and work out efficiency from them.
intro: Every time you move, eat, switch on a light or light a fire, energy is doing something. It shifts from one place to another, changes form, or spreads out. But physics tells us the total never changes. Energy cannot be made from nothing, and it never disappears. Knowing where energy is stored and how it moves is the base of everything in physics. That includes engines, power stations, diet science and even climate change. It is tested on every paper, so getting it right now pays off hugely.

keyPoints.heading: The eight energy stores
keyPoints.content: There are eight separate energy stores. You need to name them and give an example of each. - Kinetic: any moving object. For example, a car, a kicked ball or a running person. - Gravitational potential: any object raised above the ground. For example, a book on a shelf, or a roller coaster at the top of a hill. - Elastic potential: a stretched or squashed object. For example, a spring, a drawn bow or a squashed rubber ball. - Thermal: any object with heat. For example, a hot cup of tea, the Sun or your own body. - Chemical: stored in bonds. For example, food, fuels (petrol, wood) and batteries. - Nuclear: stored in the nuclei of atoms. For example, uranium, or the Sun's core. - Electrostatic: between charged objects. For example, static on a balloon, or the charge between a thundercloud and the ground. - Magnetic: between magnets or magnetic materials. For example, two magnets attracting or repelling.
writeBullets: Kinetic — any moving object
Gravitational potential — any object at height
Elastic potential — stretched or squashed objects
Thermal — any object with heat energy
Chemical — food, fuels, batteries (stored in bonds)
Nuclear — stored inside atomic nuclei
Electrostatic — between charged objects
Magnetic — between magnets

keyTerms.def: A way energy can be held. There are eight types: kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal, chemical, nuclear, electrostatic, magnetic
Energy stored in a moving object; calculated using Ek = ½mv², where m is mass (kg) and v is speed (m/s); measured in joules (J)
Energy stored in an object due to its height above a reference point; calculated using Ep = mgh, where g = 9.8 N/kg on Earth; measured in joules (J)
Energy stored in a stretched or compressed object; calculated using Ee = ½ke², where k is the spring constant (N/m) and e is the extension (m); measured in joules (J)

keyPoints.memTip: Use the acronym KGET-CNE-M: Kinetic, Gravitational, Elastic, Thermal, Chemical, Nuclear, Electrostatic, Magnetic. Picture a cheetah (kinetic) leaping off a cliff (gravitational). It lands on a spring (elastic) and heats up (thermal). It is powered by food (chemical), on a nuclear planet. It is struck by lightning (electrostatic) and hits a magnet (magnetic).

keyPoints.heading: The four ways energy is transferred
keyPoints.content: Energy does not just jump between stores. It is always transferred by a particular pathway. There are four: - Mechanically: by a force acting on an object, like pushing, pulling or kicking a ball. - Electrically: by an electric current moving through a circuit. - By heating: energy flows from a hotter object to a cooler one (conduction, convection, radiation). - By radiation: by electromagnetic waves (light, infrared) or by sound waves. The key wording is: 'energy is transferred [pathway] from the [store] store to the [store] store'. Practise that sentence.
writeBullets: Mechanically — by a force acting on an object
Electrically — by an electric current
By heating — from a hotter object to a cooler one
By radiation — electromagnetic waves or sound waves

keyTerms.def: Energy transferred by a force acting on an object — e.g. pushing, pulling, kicking; work is done against or by the force
Energy transferred by a moving electric charge (current) through a circuit
Energy transferred from a hotter object to a cooler one by conduction, convection, or radiation; always flows from higher to lower temperature
Energy transferred by electromagnetic waves (e.g. light, infrared) or by sound waves without requiring a medium for EM waves

keyPoints.memTip: MEHR: Mechanical, Electrical, Heating, Radiation. These are the four transfer pathways examiners expect. Practise the sentence: 'Energy is transferred [pathway] from the [store] store to the [store] store.'

keyPoints.heading: Conservation of energy — the rule that never breaks
keyPoints.content: The law of conservation of energy says that energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can only be transferred from one store to another, or dissipated (spread out). The total energy in a closed system always stays the same. This is one of the most important laws in all of science. Say you push a book off a table. The gravitational potential energy does not disappear. It becomes kinetic energy as the book falls. Then it becomes sound and thermal energy when the book hits the floor. Track it, and you will always find the same total.
writeBullets: Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can only be transferred or dissipated
Total energy in a closed system is always constant
Energy that seems to 'disappear' has been transferred to thermal energy in the surroundings
Example: a falling book. Gravitational potential → kinetic → thermal + sound on impact

keyTerms.def: Energy cannot be created or destroyed — it can only be transferred between stores or dissipated as thermal energy to the surroundings; total energy in a closed system is always constant
A system in which no energy is transferred to or from the surroundings — the total energy remains constant

keyPoints.memTip: Energy is NEVER created and NEVER destroyed. It only moves between stores or spreads out. Every energy question has the same total on both sides.

keyPoints.heading: Dissipation — where useful energy goes to die
keyPoints.content: In any real energy transfer, some energy ends up in a store that is no use. This is called dissipation. The most common dissipated form is thermal energy transferred to the surroundings. In other words, it is heat that warms the air around a machine. A car engine changes chemical energy in petrol into kinetic energy, which is useful. But some becomes sound (engine noise). Some becomes thermal energy in the exhaust and engine block. That energy is wasted. You are often asked to name the wasted energy store and explain why it is less useful. Key point: all energy eventually ends up as thermal energy in the surroundings. It becomes so spread out that it cannot be used again. That spreading out is called dissipation.
writeBullets: Dissipation = energy transferred to a store that is no use to us
Most common wasted form = thermal energy transferred to the surroundings
All energy eventually becomes thermal energy spread out in the surroundings
Dissipated energy is harder to use, because it is spread out and at a low temperature
Example: a light bulb. Electrical → light (useful) + thermal (wasted)

keyTerms.def: The spreading of energy into the thermal store of the surroundings, making it less useful — all real energy transfers dissipate some energy
Energy transferred to a store that is not useful for the intended purpose of the device — most commonly thermal energy lost to the surroundings

keyPoints.memTip: Dissipation = energy spreading out and becoming less useful. Examiners may ask 'why is this energy less useful?'. Answer: it is transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings and cannot easily be recovered.

keyPoints.heading: Sankey diagrams and efficiency
keyPoints.content: A Sankey diagram is an arrow diagram. The width of each arrow is proportional to the amount of energy. The thick arrow on the left = total energy input. It splits into arrows on the right. One wide arrow = useful energy output. One or more thinner arrows = wasted energy, usually pointing down. To work out efficiency, use: efficiency = useful output energy transfer ÷ total input energy transfer. This gives a decimal. Multiply by 100 for a percentage. It is also written as: efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input. A perfect device would have efficiency = 1.0 (or 100%). In reality it is always less, because some energy is always dissipated.
writeBullets: Sankey diagram: arrow width = amount of energy
Thick left arrow = total energy input
Wide right arrow = useful output. Thin arrow(s) = wasted energy
Efficiency = useful output energy ÷ total input energy
Multiply by 100 to get a percentage. In reality it is always less than 1.0 (or 100%)

keyTerms.def: A flow diagram where the width of each arrow is proportional to the amount of energy — the input arrow splits into useful output and wasted energy arrows
The ratio of useful output energy (or power) to total input energy (or power); efficiency = useful output ÷ total input; always between 0 and 1 (or 0% and 100%)

keyPoints.memTip: Efficiency = useful OUT ÷ total IN. It is always less than 1. Wasted energy = input − useful output.

A skier at the top of a slope
The object is raised higher or has more mass

0.question: A book sits on a high shelf. Which energy store does it have?
0.correctFeedback: Correct. The book is high up, so it has energy in its gravitational potential store. That would change to kinetic energy if it fell.
0.wrongFeedback: The book is high above the ground, so the correct store is gravitational potential. Kinetic needs movement. Elastic needs stretching or squashing. Chemical is stored in bonds, like food or fuel.

1.question: A moving car transfers energy to its surroundings when it brakes. Which transfer pathway best describes this?
options: Electrically. An electric current transfers energy to the brakes
Mechanically. The friction force between brakes and wheels transfers energy as heat
By radiation. Infrared radiation carries energy from the car to the air
Chemically. The fuel reacts with brake fluid to release energy
1.correctFeedback: Correct. When the brakes put a friction force on the wheels, energy is transferred mechanically (by a force). The energy is then dissipated as thermal energy in the brakes and surroundings.
1.wrongFeedback: Energy can be transferred in four ways. Two are mechanically (by a force) and electrically (by a current). The others are by heating (from hotter to cooler) and by radiation (waves). Braking uses a contact force, so that is mechanical transfer. The energy then becomes thermal.

2.question: A student says energy is destroyed when a ball rolls to a stop on a carpet. Why is this wrong?
options: Energy is really created when the ball stops. It turns into cold
Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It has been transferred to thermal energy in the carpet and surroundings
The ball still has kinetic energy even though it has stopped
Energy is only destroyed if the object is on a frictionless surface
2.correctFeedback: Correct. This is conservation of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed. When the ball stops, friction has transferred its kinetic energy to thermal energy (heat). That heat is in the carpet, the ball and the air around them.
2.wrongFeedback: Energy is never destroyed. The law of conservation of energy says total energy is constant. When the ball stops, its kinetic energy has been transferred to thermal energy (heat). That heat is in the carpet and surroundings. It has changed store, not disappeared.

3.question: A light bulb transfers 100 J of electrical energy. 15 J becomes light. The rest becomes thermal energy in the surroundings. Which term describes the 85 J of thermal energy?
3.correctFeedback: Correct. The 85 J transferred to the surroundings as thermal energy is dissipated energy. It is no use for the bulb's purpose, which is light. It is spread out into the surroundings, where it is hard to recover.
3.wrongFeedback: Dissipation means energy transferred to a store that is no use for the job. Most often this is thermal energy spread out in the surroundings. The 85 J of thermal energy from the bulb is dissipated energy.

4.question: A motor uses 500 J of electrical energy and does 350 J of useful work. What is its efficiency?
4.correctFeedback: Correct. Efficiency = 350 ÷ 500 = 0.70 (or 70%). The other 150 J is dissipated, usually as thermal energy.
4.wrongFeedback: Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input = 350 ÷ 500 = 0.70. If you got 1.43, you divided the wrong way round. Efficiency must always be less than 1. If you got 0.35, you divided by 1000 instead of 500.

commonMistakes: Kinetic energy belongs to moving objects. An object that is not moving has zero kinetic energy, however heavy it is.
Efficiency is always between 0 and 1 (or 0% and 100%). If your answer is more than 1, you divided input by output. Divide output by input instead.
All energy ends up as thermal energy in the surroundings. It is not 'destroyed'. If asked where wasted energy goes, say: transferred to the thermal energy store of the surroundings.
Sankey arrows that point down show wasted (dissipated) energy. The arrow pointing right (or forward) is the useful output. Find the right arrow before reading off values.
Gravitational potential energy goes up with both height AND mass. A heavier object at the same height has more GPE than a lighter one.
examTips: When describing an energy transfer, use full exam wording. Say: 'Energy is transferred [pathway] from the [store] store to the [store] store'. The pathway is mechanically, electrically, by heating or by radiation. This wording earns marks.

For Sankey diagram calculations, first read off the input and useful output values. Use the arrow widths or the numbers given. Then efficiency = useful output ÷ input. To find wasted energy: input − useful output.
You may be asked to 'explain why a device is not 100% efficient'. Say: some energy is dissipated as thermal energy to the surroundings and cannot be recovered.
